text: Every group-by-tag and filter-by-tag workflow from the last lesson rests on one assumption: the tag has to exist, and it has to be written the same way every time. A team tag spelled three different ways across three resource groups doesn't group into one bucket in Cost Analysis or Cost Explorer — it fragments into three, and a resource with no tag at all just falls into an untagged bucket nobody's accountable for. Tagging strategy isn't a nice-to-have on top of FinOps; it's the mechanism that makes the Inform phase actually work.

Most organizations converge on a small, consistent set of tag keys rather than letting every team invent its own. Four keys show up constantly, as an illustrative starting point to adapt rather than copy exactly: team or owner, for who's accountable; project or cost-center, for which budget line the spend rolls up to; environment, separating production from staging and dev in every report; and application, grouping resources in the same logical service. The value isn't the exact taxonomy — it's consistency. Five keys every resource actually carries beats twenty keys half the resources are missing.

Writing that convention into a wiki page doesn't make it hold under deadline pressure, so Azure enforces it with Azure Policy instead. A built-in policy requiring a specific tag and value can be assigned at the subscription or management group scope with a Deny effect, so deploying a resource without that tag gets rejected outright at deployment time, not flagged in a report a week later. Policy can also append an inherited tag automatically from a resource group, cutting down how often anyone has to type it by hand.

AWS does the equivalent through AWS Organizations tag policies, attached to an organizational unit or the whole organization. A tag policy defines which keys are required, which capitalization is enforced, and which values are allowed, then reports — or can be configured to prevent — any resource that violates it. And remember the last lesson's detail: enforcing that a tag exists is a separate step from activating it as a Cost Allocation Tag in Billing, which is still required before Cost Explorer will group or filter by it.

With a consistent, enforced taxonomy in place, cost allocation across teams and projects finally becomes reliable instead of accidental. The next lesson puts that reliable data to work proactively — setting Azure Budgets and AWS Budgets with anomaly detection, so a cost spike gets caught within days instead of showing up as a surprise on the monthly bill.
